analysis.one_liner: Requires federal agencies to buy goods and services from private companies instead of doing the work themselves.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have made private contracting the default for federal work, was referred to committee in December 2019, drew zero cosponsors, and died without any committee or floor action when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required every federal executive, military, and independent agency to obtain its goods and services from private companies rather than perform them with federal employees. Exemptions would exist only where the law requires government workers, where the work is critical or inherently governmental, where national defense or homeland security requires it, or where no private company can do it. Agencies could keep work in-house only after a formal cost study showing federal employees give taxpayers the best value, and the White House budget office would have to file an annual report with a schedule for transferring commercial work to the private sector within five years. The bill never advanced past its initial committee referral and expired at the end of the 116th Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Private federal contractors would gain the most: the bill would flip the default so that outsourcing is the rule and in-house federal work is the exception that must be formally justified, with a mandated five-year schedule for shifting commercial activities to private firms. Companies in defense support, information technology, facilities management, and other federal service lines would gain a steady pipeline of work now done by government employees.

how_it_helps.text: Each agency would be required to obtain all goods and services needed for its functions from private sources, with only narrow exemptions such as work required by law to be done by the agency, national defense or homeland security needs, inherently governmental work, or cases where no private source exists.

Work not exempted would move to the private sector through divestiture of federal involvement, competitively awarded contracts, or a cost study finding that private provision gives taxpayers the best value.

The Office of Management and Budget would have to study every agency's activities annually and send Congress a report including a schedule for transferring commercial activities to the private sector within five years.
The Office of Management and Budget's regulations would also require states and localities to follow the same privatization policy when spending federal funds.

analysis.who_pays: Federal employees would bear the risk, since their jobs could be shifted to contractors under the five-year transfer schedule. Taxpayers would bear the cost if contracted work ends up costing more than in-house work once contractor profit margins, contract administration, and oversight are counted. People who rely on federal services could face lower quality if work moves to firms that answer to profit rather than to the public.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal employees, taxpayers, and public services

drawbacks.text: The bill makes contracting the legal default and requires agencies to justify keeping any work in-house, removing the discretion agencies currently have to decide the best way to deliver services; exemptions are available only if the agency head certifies them to Congress under Office of Management and Budget rules.

Private provision is not automatically cheaper: contract awards add contractor profit margins and government contract-administration costs on top of the work itself, and public-private cost studies have historically produced mixed savings results, so the bill's core assumption that private firms are always the best value is not guaranteed.

The mandate would extend beyond federal agencies: states and localities spending federal money would have to implement the same privatization policy, reducing their flexibility over how to deliver services.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated case is that competitive private firms are more productive and efficient, and in some cases that is true. But the bill does not simply allow outsourcing where it makes sense; it mandates it, treating every federal activity as commercial unless an agency head can certify an exception and Congress is notified, and it requires an affirmative five-year transfer schedule. That structure would lock contractors into a permanent role delivering federal work and put the burden of proof on the public workforce rather than on the contractors, even though the cost savings the policy assumes are not assured once profit margins and contract oversight are counted.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in December 2019 and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator John Thune introduced the bill on December 5, 2019, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.
No cosponsors ever signed on to the bill.
The committee took no further action, no markup or vote was ever scheduled, and the bill received no floor consideration before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, nothing changed: federal agencies kept their in-house workforce and their discretion over how work gets done, and contractors gained no new legal presumption in their favor. Federal employees and the public's interest in accountable, directly provided government services came out ahead relative to where the bill would have put them.

for.name: Sen. John Thune
for.role: U.S. Senator from South Dakota; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee

against.name: Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred; chaired by Sen. Ron Johnson (R-WI)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup, vote, or any further action after referral

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no recorded votes, so no partisan split ever formed around it.

industries.note: The bill would make private procurement the legal default for nearly all federal work and require a five-year schedule for transferring commercial activities to contractors, directing public dollars and public jobs to these firms. Contractor profit margins and contract administration can raise the total cost to taxpayers compared with in-house federal work, and the firms would gain work they must win on the merits today.

industries.industry: Federal employee workforce and public-sector labor
industries.note: Federal employees' jobs would be subject to outsourcing under a mandated transfer schedule, and they could keep work in-house only after a formal study showing best value. Their interest in keeping work in-house runs alongside the public's interest in accountable, directly provided government services.

Under the bill's regulatory language, states and localities spending federal funds would have to implement the same privatization policy, constraining how they deliver services. They would lose flexibility, though the bill would not directly fund or defund them.
